recall_prompt: Say how you would answer all three parts — which domain each one uses, and what the operation does to the images.

steps.label: Find the domains
steps.margin_note: One of the four marks, and the decision that governs all three parts. f + 4 and f³ keep f's own domain {4, 5, 6}; only f/g is cut down to the intersection {4, 6}.
steps.memory_tip: One function alone keeps its own domain. Two functions together need the intersection.

recall.must_convey: That f + 4 and f³ keep f's own domain {4, 5, 6}, while f/g uses the intersection {4, 6} with the zeros of g removed.
accept: f plus four and f cubed use f alone so the domain stays four five six
f by g needs both functions so take the intersection four and six
the domain of a quotient also needs g not equal to zero
f okkate unte f domain, rendu unte intersection teesukovali
two of the parts keep f's domain and only the quotient is cut down
reject: the union is four five six and eight

steps.why: The domain decides which preimages appear in each answer, and it is not the same for the three parts. Two of them use f alone; only the quotient needs both functions.
common_mistakes: Using the intersection {4, 6} for f + 4 and f³ as well.

steps.label: Find f + 4
steps.margin_note: The second mark. Add 4 to the image only. The pair (6, 0) stays, because a value of zero is still a value.
steps.memory_tip: Add 4 to the second coordinate only. The inputs 4, 5 and 6 do not move.

recall.must_convey: That 4 is added to each image, leaving the first coordinates alone: f + 4 = {(4, 9), (5, 10), (6, 0)}.
accept: add four to every image so you get four nine five ten and six zero
the inputs stay the same and four is added to each output
f plus four is four comma nine five comma ten six comma zero
second coordinate ki four add cheyyali, inputs marave
the pair at six becomes zero and it is still kept
reject: the domain is the intersection four and six

steps.why: The 4 here is the constant function 4, which is defined for every real number, so it takes nothing away from f's domain. Only the second coordinate changes.
common_mistakes: Adding 4 to the first coordinate as well.
Dropping the pair (6, 0) because the value is zero.

steps.label: Find f/g
steps.margin_note: The third mark. Two conditions, not one: both functions defined, and g not zero. Check g(4) and g(6) in writing before dividing.
steps.memory_tip: For f/g check two things at each point: both functions defined, and g not zero.
lines: Neither is 0, so both pairs are kept.

recall.must_convey: That on the intersection {4, 6} neither g value is zero, so f/g = {(4, −5/4), (6, −4/5)}.
accept: on four and six g is minus four and five and neither is zero so both pairs stay
f by g is four comma minus five by four and six comma minus four by five
divide the image of f by the image of g at each shared point
g zero kaadu kabatti rendu pairs untai
the quotient is minus five by four and minus four by five
reject: the domain of f is four five six

steps.why: A quotient needs the bottom function to be non zero as well as defined, so the domain of f/g is the intersection with the zeros of g removed. Nothing extra is removed here, but the check still has to be written.
common_mistakes: Writing the quotient at 5 or 8, where one of the two functions is undefined.
Dividing g by f instead of f by g.

steps.label: Find f³
steps.margin_note: The fourth mark. f³ cubes the IMAGE. A cube keeps the sign, so (−4)³ = −64, not 64.
steps.memory_tip: f³ cubes the image, and a cube keeps the sign: (−4)³ = −64.

steps.why: f³ means the image cubed, not f composed with itself three times. A cube keeps the sign, so the negative image stays negative — unlike f², where it would not.
common_mistakes: Reading f³ as fofof, the composition.
